issues.legal_issue: Commercial shrimp farms are prohibited within the coastal regulation zone unless they use traditional or improved traditional methods.
material_facts: The coastal regulation notification prohibited specified activities within the coastal regulation zone and permitted only listed uses in the relevant coastal classification.
Commercial shrimp farms require brackish water, which can be supplied from sources other than the immediate shore, and do not require foreshore facilities.
Reports documented that commercial shrimp farming degraded coastal ecology, polluted water, damaged land and mangroves, and restricted traditional fishing access.
The court found that traditional and improved traditional aquaculture methods were environmentally benign, while other identified methods caused pollution and environmental degradation.
issues.conclusion: Shrimp farms are covered by the prohibition on new industries within the coastal regulation zone and cannot be established there, except for traditional and improved traditional methods.
issues.legal_principle: The coastal regulation notification issued under Section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 prohibits new industries in the coastal regulation zone unless they are directly related to the waterfront or directly need foreshore facilities. The court held that commercial shrimp farming meets neither exception merely because it uses brackish water. It also relied on the notification's prohibition on bunding or disturbing the natural course of seawater and its specified permissible uses, and on the distinction between traditional and improved traditional methods and other methods described in the Alagarswami report.

predicates.public_interest_environment_proceeding: A public-interest proceeding seeks enforcement of coastal environmental protections against aquaculture activity.
predicates.shrimp_farm_within_coastal_regulation_zo: A shrimp farm is situated within the regulated coastal zone.
predicates.commercial_nontraditional_method: The farm uses a commercial method other than a traditional or improved traditional method.

issues.definition: When a public-interest environmental proceeding concerns a commercial, nontraditional shrimp farm in the regulated coastal zone, the rule bars that farm from operating there.

issues.legal_issue: A central environmental notification issued under the Environment (Protection) Act prevails over inconsistent state legislation.
material_facts: State legislation regulating coastal aquaculture was argued to permit activities inconsistent with the central coastal regulation notification.
The notification was issued under the Environment (Protection) Act, a central law enacted to implement decisions of an international environmental conference.
issues.conclusion: The central environmental law and the notification made under it override inconsistent state legislation.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, enacted under Entry 13 of List I read with Article 253 of the Constitution, to implement international environmental decisions. A notification made under that Act has overriding effect over inconsistent state legislation.

predicates.public_interest_environment_proceeding: A public-interest proceeding concerns the regulation of activities affecting the coastal environment.
predicates.state_coastal_law_conflicts_with_central: A state law permits or regulates a coastal activity inconsistently with a central environmental notification.

issues.definition: In a public-interest environmental proceeding, an inconsistency between state coastal legislation and a central environmental notification results in the central notification prevailing.

issues.legal_issue: Commercial aquaculture outside the coastal regulation zone and specified sensitive-lake exclusion areas requires prior approval and must not cause specified environmental harms.
material_facts: The court found that commercial and other nontraditional shrimp farming had caused pollution, salinisation of soil and drinking water, harmful sedimentation, and damage to local fauna and flora.
The reports showed that the environmental and social damage from aquaculture in fragile coastal areas could exceed the economic benefits.

The court directed that nontraditional aquaculture outside the coastal regulation zone and outside specified lake exclusion areas could be established only with the approval of the authority it ordered to be constituted.
issues.conclusion: Nontraditional aquaculture outside the coastal regulation zone and the specified lake exclusion areas may be established only with prior approval, and activities causing the identified environmental harms must not be allowed.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the precautionary principle and the requirement of environmental scrutiny before permission is granted. It relied on the environmental impact assessments and the evidence of salinity, pollution, sedimentation, and ecological harm, and required an authority to assess proposed commercial aquaculture and its environmental effects before authorising it.

predicates.public_interest_environment_proceeding: A public-interest proceeding seeks control of aquaculture activity because of its effects on the environment.
predicates.nontraditional_aquaculture_outside_prote: A nontraditional aquaculture operation is proposed outside the regulated coastal zone and the specified sensitive-lake exclusion areas.
predicates.proposed_activity_requires_environmental: The proposed operation presents potential environmental effects requiring scrutiny before it is allowed to proceed.

issues.definition: When nontraditional aquaculture is proposed outside protected zones in a proceeding addressing its environmental risks, it must undergo prior environmental authorisation.

issues.legal_issue: The precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle apply as part of environmental law.
material_facts: The record contained reports of untreated or inadequately treated effluent, contaminated water and soil, damaged mangroves, and harm to fishing and farming livelihoods.
The court relied on evidence that ecological and social damage from commercial aquaculture could exceed its economic benefits.
Earlier decisions of the court had accepted the precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle as part of environmental law.
issues.conclusion: The precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle are part of the environmental law of the country.
issues.legal_principle: Relying on Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India, the court held that environmental measures must anticipate, prevent, and address environmental degradation; scientific uncertainty does not justify postponing measures against a threat of serious or irreversible harm; and the developer bears the burden of showing its action is environmentally benign. Relying also on Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India, it held that polluters are liable for environmental harm and the cost of restoring damaged ecology.

predicates.public_interest_environment_proceeding: A public-interest proceeding asks the court to address activity affecting the environment.
predicates.activity_threatens_environmental_harm: The activity presents a threat of environmental degradation or has caused environmental harm.

issues.definition: When a public-interest environmental proceeding concerns an activity that threatens or causes environmental harm, the precautionary and polluter-pays principles apply.

issues.legal_issue: An operator responsible for pollution must compensate affected people and pay the cost of restoring the damaged environment.
material_facts: Reports attributed pollution, salinisation, ecological degradation, and loss of livelihood to commercial aquaculture operations.
The court found that commercial aquaculture farms had operated in coastal areas in violation of applicable environmental requirements and that affected people had suffered harm.
The court directed an authority to assess both the loss to ecology and the compensation owed to affected individuals and families, with recovery from polluters.
issues.conclusion: Polluting aquaculture operators are liable to compensate affected people and to pay the cost of restoring the damaged environment.
issues.legal_principle: Under the polluter-pays principle, as explained in Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India and Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India, liability extends beyond compensation to victims to the cost of reversing environmental degradation. The court also applied the principle of absolute liability for harm caused by hazardous or inherently dangerous activity.

predicates.public_interest_environment_proceeding: A public-interest proceeding seeks relief for environmental pollution or degradation.
predicates.operator_activity_causes_pollution_harm: An operator's activity causes pollution or environmental harm.
predicates.affected_people_or_ecology_suffer_loss: People or the environment suffer loss as a result of the pollution or harm.

issues.definition: When an operator's activity causes pollution and resulting loss in a public-interest environmental proceeding, the operator must compensate those affected and fund restoration.

issues.legal_issue: Agricultural, salt-pan, mangrove, wetland, forest, village-common, and public-purpose lands must not be converted for shrimp-farm construction.
material_facts: The reports documented the conversion of agricultural and salt-production lands into commercial aquaculture farms and the destruction of mangrove areas.
The reports linked these changes to loss of cultivable land, livelihoods, potable water, and ecological resources.
The court expressly directed that the listed categories of land not be used or converted for shrimp-farm construction.
issues.conclusion: The specified agricultural, salt-pan, ecological, common, and public-purpose lands cannot be used or converted for shrimp-farm construction.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the precautionary principle and its findings that conversion of these lands caused environmental degradation and harm to local livelihoods. It ordered protection of the identified land categories as part of its environmental directions.

predicates.public_interest_environment_proceeding: A public-interest proceeding addresses environmental effects of shrimp farming.
predicates.land_is_protected_land_category: The land is agricultural, salt-production, mangrove, wetland, forest, village-common, or intended for a public purpose.
predicates.land_proposed_for_shrimp_farm_conversion: The land is proposed to be used or converted for construction of a shrimp farm.

issues.definition: When protected land is proposed for conversion to shrimp-farm use in a public-interest environmental proceeding, that conversion is barred.

issues.legal_issue: Aquaculture operations within the specified exclusion distance of protected lakes and bird sanctuaries must not be established and existing operations there must be closed.
material_facts: The reports described harm to sensitive lake ecosystems, bird habitats, and water flows associated with shrimp farming.
The court found that the specified lake and sanctuary areas required protection from aquaculture activity.
The court ordered that no aquaculture operation be established within the specified exclusion distance and that existing operations within it be closed and demolished.
issues.conclusion: Aquaculture operations are prohibited within the specified exclusion distance of the protected lakes and associated bird sanctuaries, and existing operations in that area must be closed.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the precautionary principle to ecologically sensitive areas and relied on the evidence of ecological damage to protected lakes and bird habitats. It imposed a specific protective exclusion as part of its remedial directions.

predicates.public_interest_environment_proceeding: A public-interest proceeding seeks protection of ecologically sensitive areas from aquaculture impacts.
predicates.aquaculture_operation_within_sensitive_l: An aquaculture operation is situated within the court-defined exclusion area around a protected lake or associated bird sanctuary.

issues.definition: When an aquaculture operation is located within the protected exclusion area in a public-interest environmental proceeding, it must not continue there.

issues.legal_issue: The central government must establish a specialised authority to protect fragile coastal areas and implement environmental principles in relation to aquaculture.
material_facts: The record showed widespread noncompliance with coastal environmental requirements and inadequate monitoring and enforcement by responsible authorities.
The court found that commercial aquaculture had caused serious environmental and social harms in coastal areas.

The court directed the central government to constitute an authority with environmental and aquaculture expertise and powers to issue directions and implement the precautionary and polluter-pays principles.
issues.conclusion: A specialised authority must be constituted with the powers necessary to protect ecologically fragile coastal areas and address the effects of aquaculture.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 empowers the central government to constitute an authority, and Section 5 empowers the issuance of directions. The court relied on those provisions and the precautionary and polluter-pays principles to require a specialised body capable of environmental scrutiny, enforcement, and remediation.

predicates.public_interest_environment_proceeding: A public-interest proceeding seeks protection of coastal environments from harmful activity.
predicates.existing_environmental_enforcement_inade: Existing authorities have failed to provide adequate monitoring or enforcement of environmental requirements.
predicates.coastal_activity_causes_significant_envi: An activity in coastal areas creates significant environmental risks or has caused substantial environmental harm.

issues.definition: When existing enforcement is inadequate and coastal activity creates significant environmental risk in a public-interest proceeding, a specialised coastal environmental authority is required.

issues.legal_issue: Eligible workmen whose employment ends because shrimp industries are closed under the court's directions are entitled to statutory retrenchment compensation and additional compensation.
material_facts: The court ordered the closure of shrimp industries in specified areas.
Workmen employed in industries required to close were in continuous service for the qualifying period described by the court.
The court directed that eligible workmen be treated as retrenched and paid compensation under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, together with additional compensation and any gratuity due.
issues.conclusion: Eligible workmen affected by the ordered closures must receive statutory retrenchment compensation, additional compensation, and any gratuity due.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the retrenchment provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 to workmen in continuous service for the qualifying period, treating them as retrenched because their industries were closed pursuant to the court's order.

predicates.court_ordered_industry_closure: A court directs that an industry be closed.
predicates.workman_employed_in_closing_industry: A workman is employed in an industry that must close under the court's direction.
predicates.workman_meets_continuous_service_require: The workman has completed the required period of continuous service before the closure.

issues.definition: When a court-ordered closure ends the employment of a workman who meets the continuous-service requirement, the workman is entitled to retrenchment and additional compensation.
